Bifactor Model Dimensionality and Reliability Indices

Source: R/bifactor_indices.R
bifactor_indices.Rd

Computes the indices that describe how much of the common variance of a scale's items, and of the variance of its total and subscale scores, a general factor accounts for beside the group factors of its subscales (Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland, 2016): the explained common variance (ECV), coefficient omega and omega hierarchical (omega_H) for the general factor, omega hierarchical subscale (omega_HS) for each group factor, the percentage of uncontaminated correlations (PUC), and the index those authors call coefficient H, the closed form of Hancock and Mueller (2001) applied to one factor's loadings, which counts the other factors' common variance as uncorrelated error and so is not the maximal reliability of the factor under the fitted model; that maximal reliability is returned beside the table. The input is a fitted bifactor model in which one general factor loads on every item and each item loads on at most one of two or more orthogonal group factors. fa_bifactor fits such a model and reports these indices with delta method intervals, with omega, omega_H, and omega_HS for the sum of the items as scored rather than of the standardized items (see Details).

Usage

bifactor_indices(
  fit,
  general = NULL,
  denominator = c("model_implied", "observed")
)

Arguments

fit

A fitted bifactor lavaan model: one general factor on all items plus two or more orthogonal group factors, each item on one group factor at most. An item on no group factor is on the general factor alone: it counts in the general factor's indices and in PUC, and in no subscale. An item listed under two or more group factors is refused unless all but one of those loadings are held at zero, fixed (0*item) or constrained (a*item with a == 0); such a loading describes the same model as leaving the item off that factor. The factors must be orthogonal (the bifactor specification), and a fit that correlates any two of them is refused. Residual covariances among the items are allowed and enter the model implied denominators. A fit with fewer than two group factors, a multiple-group fit, a multilevel fit, and a fit whose optimizer did not converge are refused (see Details).

general

Optional name of the general factor. When NULL (default) the general factor is detected as the one that loads on every item.

denominator

How the total-score variance in the denominators of omega, omega_H, and omega_HS is estimated: "model_implied" (the default; the variance the fitted bifactor model reproduces, as in Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland, 2016, with any residual covariances the model specifies) or "observed" (the variance of the composite estimated from the data, the denominator of robust omega in reliability_omega). For a fit to ordered items both describe the sum of the latent responses, not of the summed categories. See Details.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_tbl) with one row per factor (the general factor first, then each group factor) and columns factor, ECV, omega, omega_H, omega_HS, PUC, and H. Quantities that do not apply to a row are NA (for example omega_H and PUC on a group factor). On a group factor's row, ECV is the general factor's share of the common variance of that factor's items and omega is the reliability of their total score (see Details); H is the index of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) on every row. The "improper" attribute flags a Heywood solution, the "maximal_reliability" attribute holds the maximal reliability the fitted model implies for each factor (a vector named by factor, in the order of the rows; NA for an improper solution), the "denominator" attribute records the denominator setting, and the "metric" attribute records the metric of the items the indices describe: "observed" for continuous items, "latent_response" for ordered items, whose coefficients describe the sum of the latent responses.

Details

Let \(\lambda^g_i\) be item \(i\)'s standardized loading on the general factor, \(\lambda^s_i\) its loading on its group factor (0 for an item on the general factor alone), and \(\theta_i\) its standardized residual variance. With orthogonal factors the overall ECV is \(\sum_i (\lambda^g_i)^2 / \sum_i [(\lambda^g_i)^2 + (\lambda^s_i)^2]\); omega and omega_H share the total-score variance \((\sum_i \lambda^g_i)^2 + \sum_g (\sum_{i \in g} \lambda^s_i)^2 + \sum_i \theta_i\) as denominator, with the general part \((\sum_i \lambda^g_i)^2\) in the numerator of omega_H. Each group factor's omega_HS uses the analogous numerator and that subscale's own total variance. PUC is one minus the share of item pairs that fall within the same group factor. Omega_H against omega says how much of the total score's reliable variance is due to the general factor; omega_HS against a subscale's omega says how much of the subscale score's reliable variance is its own, beyond the total; ECV and PUC describe how close the items come to measuring one thing. The table reports the numbers; whether a total or subscale score is worth reporting is the researcher's judgment, and the package draws no line, as on the page of fa_bifactor.

The metric of omega. The loadings and residual variances above are standardized, so omega, omega_H, and omega_HS describe the sum of the standardized items, as Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) write them. fa_bifactor reports them for the sum of the items as scored, the coefficients fa_confirmatory and semTools::compRelSEM() compute. The two agree when the items have equal variances and differ otherwise: in the first example below, whose items have nearly equal variances, omega_H is 0.67348 here and 0.67305 for the sum of the items as scored, while on the 15 tests of the example of fa_bifactor, whose variances range from 8.0 to 153.3, it is 0.577 here and 0.552 there. ECV, H, the maximal reliability, and PUC do not differ.

A group factor's row. The row of group factor \(s\) describes its items, the subscale \(s\), and its ECV and omega are not the general row's quantities restricted to a group factor. Its ECV is the general factor's share of the subscale's common variance, $$\frac{\sum_{i \in s} (\lambda^g_i)^2} {\sum_{i \in s} [(\lambda^g_i)^2 + (\lambda^s_i)^2]},$$ so one minus it is the group factor's own share of that variance, and a high value says the subscale's common variance is mostly general (it goes with a low omega_HS). It is not the group factor's share of the common variance of all the items, which is \(\sum_{i \in s} (\lambda^s_i)^2\) over the denominator of the overall ECV. Its omega is the omega of the subscale's total score, \((\sum_{i \in s} \lambda^g_i)^2 + (\sum_{i \in s} \lambda^s_i)^2\) over that score's variance, the reliability of the subscale score with both factors counted as true score; omega_HS keeps only the group factor's part of the numerator. Its H is the index described next, computed from the group factor's loadings. The printed table states what ECV and omega mean on these rows.

Coefficient H. The column H is the index Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) report: the closed form of Hancock and Mueller (2001), $$H = \frac{\sum_i \lambda_i^2 / (1 - \lambda_i^2)} {1 + \sum_i \lambda_i^2 / (1 - \lambda_i^2)},$$ over the general loadings for the general factor and over a group factor's loadings for that factor. It counts \(1 - \lambda_i^2\) as item \(i\)'s error variance, and so treats the variance an item shares with the other factors as error that is uncorrelated across items. In a bifactor model that variance is correlated (the items of a subscale share their group factor, and every item shares the general factor), so the index is not the maximal reliability of the factor under the fitted model, which is what reliability_H computes for a block of items whose errors are correlated (Gabler & Raykov, 2017). That maximal reliability is \(\lambda_f' R^{-1} \lambda_f\), where \(\lambda_f\) holds the factor's standardized loadings (zero for an item off the factor) and \(R\) is the item correlation matrix the model reproduces: the squared multiple correlation of the factor with all of the items, the largest reliability any weighted sum of them reaches as a measure of that factor, and the square of the determinacy of its regression factor score in factor_scores. It is returned as the "maximal_reliability" attribute and printed under the table, and ci_bifactor_indices gives it a confidence interval, as it does every index of the table but PUC, which depends on the model's structure alone.

The two differ in either direction, and what sets the direction is not the same on the two kinds of row. On the general factor's row the index counts the group factors' variance as uncorrelated error, but the items of a subscale share it. When the loadings on each group factor are positive and similar, no weighting of the items removes that shared variance without removing general variance with it, and the index is the larger: in the first example below it is 0.769 for the general factor, whose maximal reliability is 0.678, barely above its omega_H of 0.673, so no weighting of the items reaches 0.769. When an item is nearly a pure indicator of its group factor, or a group factor's loadings differ in sign, a weighting can cancel group variance that the index counts as error, and the maximal reliability is the larger. On a group factor's row the index counts the general factor's variance, with the unique variance, as uncorrelated error. When the subscale's own items have proportional loadings on the two factors (equal loadings, for instance), no weighting of them alone removes the general factor without removing the group factor with it, but the optimal weights use every item, and the items of the other subscales measure the general factor and nothing of this group factor, so the weights use them to remove it. The better those items measure the general factor, the closer the maximal reliability comes to the closed form above with each item's unique variance \(\theta_i\) in place of \(1 - (\lambda^s_i)^2\), which is above the index. Which of the two prevails depends on the general loadings, the group loadings, and the number of items outside the subscale together, not on the sign and similarity of the group loadings alone. In a population of nine items in three subscales of three, with every general loading .7 and every group loading .3 (an ECV of .84), the index is 0.229 for each group factor and its maximal reliability 0.279, while for the general factor they are 0.896 and 0.865; with general and group loadings of .5, as in the first example below, the index is the larger on every row (0.500 against 0.471 for a group factor in the population); and with two subscales of six items, general loadings .8, and group loadings .4, the index is the larger for a group factor (0.533 against 0.468), although the general factor is stronger than in the first population.

The composite that reaches a group factor's maximal reliability is the factor's regression score from all of the items, and it weights the items of the other subscales negatively: in the first population the optimal weights are proportional to 1 for each of the subscale's three items and -0.405 for each of the other six. No score of the subscale's own items reaches that reliability. The best weighting of them alone reaches \(\lambda_s' R_{ss}^{-1} \lambda_s\), with \(\lambda_s\) their group loadings and \(R_{ss}\) their correlations, which is omega_HS when the items have equal loadings on both factors, and then below the index as well: 0.125 in the first population, against an index of 0.229 and a maximal reliability of 0.279. So a maximal reliability above the index on a group factor's row, which is common when the items outside the subscale measure a strong general factor well (a profile of high ECV, in which the subscale rows are commonly consulted), describes a factor score computed from all of the items, not the subscale score; how much of a subscale score's variance is due to its group factor is omega_HS. Read the column as the published index, comparable with values reported beside it, and the attribute as the reliability that optimal weights of all of the items could reach in the population. The sample values of both overstate their population values on average, the attribute most of all for a weakly determined group factor, and a composite weighted with sample estimates reaches less, as Aguirre-Urreta, Rönkkö, and McIntosh (2019) found for H of a single factor; ci_bifactor_indices gives the bootstrap estimate of that bias with the intervals.

The H of a factor any of whose standardized loadings is at or beyond one in absolute value is NA, since the index then gives that item an error variance that is not positive.

Each denominator is the sum of the corresponding block of an item correlation matrix on the standardized metric of the loadings: all items for omega and omega_H, a group factor's items for its omega_HS. The default (denominator = "model_implied") takes the correlation matrix the fitted model reproduces. For an orthogonal bifactor model without residual covariances that block sum is the total-score variance written above, the form given by Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016); when the model also specifies residual covariances among the items, the block sum carries each of them as well, since they are part of the variance of the composite the model reproduces, although not of its common variance, so the numerators leave them out. With denominator = "observed" the matrix is instead the item correlation matrix estimated from the data (lavaan's sample statistics, which under missing = "ml" are the full information estimates). This is the denominator of robust omega (reliability_omega) carried to the bifactor coefficients: it estimates the variance of the composite consistently whether or not the bifactor model reproduces it, while the numerators remain model based. When the model reproduces the item correlations the two settings agree, and a gap between them shows that it does not reproduce the composite variance. The printed table names the denominator in a line under the table.

The indices assume uncorrelated factors: a correlation between the general factor and a group factor, or between two group factors, is common variance that belongs to neither, and the partition behind ECV, omega_H, and omega_HS has no place for it. A fit that estimates such a correlation is refused with an error naming the pair.

A fit with one group factor. A general factor beside a single group factor is not a bifactor model with subscales: its indices would divide the common variance between those two factors alone, every item would belong to the one subscale, and PUC would be 0. Such a fit is refused, as fa_bifactor and ci_bifactor_indices refuse it, with a message that names the group factor. A general factor with one further factor can be fitted with lavaan::cfa() and read from its own parameter estimates.

Ordered-categorical items. For a fit with ordered indicators (WLSMV or DWLS on polychoric correlations), lavaan's sample statistics are the polychoric correlations, and the standardized loadings are on the metric of the continuous latent responses behind the categories. Both settings then give the reliability of the sum of those latent responses, not of the summed category scores a user computes, and categorization lowers reliability, often substantially (Green & Yang, 2009, Table 1). The printed line says which metric the denominator is on, and the "metric" attribute records it. For a single factor, reliability_omega_categorical gives the reliability of the summed categories; DMAR does not compute the bifactor indices on that metric.

A bifactor model that is over-parameterized for the data frequently yields an improper (Heywood) solution, a standardized loading outside \([-1, 1]\) or a negative residual variance, whose indices are not trustworthy. When that happens the indices are still returned but a warning is issued and the "improper" attribute is set to TRUE; H is NA for a factor with a loading at or beyond one, as described above, and the maximal reliability is NA for every factor, since it is not defined for an improper solution.

A fit whose optimizer did not converge (lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "converged") is FALSE, as when it reached its iteration limit) is not a solution, proper or improper: its estimates mark where the optimizer stopped. It is refused with an error of class dmar_not_converged, as ci_bifactor_indices refuses it.

One group and one level. The standardized loadings and residual variances of a fit are those of one group at one level: each group of a multiple-group fit has its own, standardized by that group's variances, so the factors have indices in each group, and neither an unweighted mean nor a mean weighted by group size is the index of any group. A multiple-group fit is refused, as average_variance_extracted refuses it, with an error of class dmar_argument_invalid that names the groups (as groups); the indices of one group are those of the model fitted to that group's data alone (which drops any equality constraints across groups). A multilevel fit, whose loadings and residual variances differ by level, is refused with an error of the same class; the standardized solution of each level is in lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "std").

References

Aguirre-Urreta, M. I., Rönkkö, M., & McIntosh, C. N. (2019). A cautionary note on the finite sample behavior of maximal reliability. Psychological Methods, 24(2), 236–252. doi:10.1037/met0000176

Gabler, S., & Raykov, T. (2017). Evaluation of maximal reliability for unidimensional measuring instruments with correlated errors. Structural Equation Modeling, 24(1), 104–111. doi:10.1080/10705511.2016.1159916

Green, S. B., & Yang, Y. (2009). Reliability of summed item scores using structural equation modeling: An alternative to coefficient alpha. Psychometrika, 74, 155–167. doi:10.1007/s11336-008-9099-3

Hancock, G. R., & Mueller, R. O. (2001). Rethinking construct reliability within latent variable systems. In R. Cudeck, S. du Toit, & D. Sörbom (Eds.), Structural equation modeling: Present and future (pp. 195–216). Scientific Software International.

Reise, S. P. (2012). The rediscovery of bifactor measurement models. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 47(5), 667–696. doi:10.1080/00273171.2012.715555

Rodriguez, A., Reise, S. P., & Haviland, M. G. (2016). Evaluating bifactor models: Calculating and interpreting statistical indices. Psychological Methods, 21(2), 137–150. doi:10.1037/met0000045

See also

fa_bifactor, which fits the bifactor model and gives these indices delta method intervals; ci_bifactor_indices for bootstrap confidence intervals for these indices and for the maximal reliability of each factor; reliability_omega, reliability_H, and factor_scores, whose regression score determinacy is the square root of the maximal reliability.

Examples

# Nine items: one general factor and three orthogonal group factors.
set.seed(113)
n <- 600
g <- rnorm(n); grp <- list(rnorm(n), rnorm(n), rnorm(n))
X <- vapply(1:9, function(i)
  0.5 * g + 0.5 * grp[[ceiling(i / 3)]] + sqrt(0.5) * rnorm(n), numeric(n))
colnames(X) <- paste0("x", 1:9)
model <- "g  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9
          f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
          f2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6
          f3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9"
fit <- lavaan::cfa(model, data = as.data.frame(X),
                   orthogonal = TRUE, std.lv = TRUE)
bifactor_indices(fit)
#>  factor ECV   omega omega_H omega_HS PUC   H    
#>  g      0.547 0.858 0.673   <NA>     0.750 0.769
#>  f1     0.609 0.727 <NA>    0.280    <NA>  0.412
#>  f2     0.543 0.756 <NA>    0.345    <NA>  0.477
#>  f3     0.490 0.743 <NA>    0.377    <NA>  0.506
#> 
#> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model
#> 
#> For a group factor, ECV is the general factor's share of the common variance of that factor's items (one minus it is the group factor's share), and omega is the reliability of their total score
#> H is the index of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016), which counts the other factors' common variance as uncorrelated error; the maximal reliability the fitted model implies is g 0.678, f1 0.396, f2 0.456, f3 0.494 (attribute "maximal_reliability"; ci_bifactor_indices() gives each an interval)

# The same indices with the observed composite variances in the
# denominators; when the model reproduces the item correlations the
# two settings agree.
bifactor_indices(fit, denominator = "observed")
#>  factor ECV   omega omega_H omega_HS PUC   H    
#>  g      0.547 0.858 0.673   <NA>     0.750 0.769
#>  f1     0.609 0.727 <NA>    0.280    <NA>  0.412
#>  f2     0.543 0.756 <NA>    0.345    <NA>  0.477
#>  f3     0.490 0.743 <NA>    0.377    <NA>  0.506
#> 
#> Denominator: observed composite variance
#> 
#> For a group factor, ECV is the general factor's share of the common variance of that factor's items (one minus it is the group factor's share), and omega is the reliability of their total score
#> H is the index of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016), which counts the other factors' common variance as uncorrelated error; the maximal reliability the fitted model implies is g 0.678, f1 0.396, f2 0.456, f3 0.494 (attribute "maximal_reliability"; ci_bifactor_indices() gives each an interval)
